segments.say: In 2006, two psychologists at Washington University in St Louis, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, ran an experiment that is now one of the most cited in the science of learning. It was simple. They gave students short prose passages about topics such as the sun and sea otters, and asked them to learn them. The twist was in how they were allowed to study.

Some students read the passage four times in a row. Others read it once, and then took a test, writing down as much as they could remember, with no feedback. Then they did another test, and another. The students who were tested spent less time reading, and more time trying to recall, which many people would think is a poor use of time.

There were two follow-ups. Some students were tested after five minutes, and others after one week. The results were revealing. After five minutes, the students who had reread the passage did better. That's what most people would expect, and it's also what makes rereading feel so effective: it does work, in the short run.

show.what: Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention

segments.say: But after a week, the picture reversed. Students who had been tested repeatedly remembered about sixty-one percent of the material, compared with about forty percent for those who had reread. The students who reread had also predicted that they'd do better. They were wrong in the direction of confidence, which is what the fluency illusion does.

show.title: Recall after one week
show.label: students who practised recall remembered more than students who reread four times

segments.say: This is the pattern that keeps reappearing in the science of learning. Methods that give you an edge on tomorrow's test may leave you with little by next month. Methods that feel clumsy on the day can leave you with much more. If you only look at the short term, you'll pick the wrong method every time.
It's a result that has been repeated in laboratories and classrooms around the world. And it's reassuring to know that it isn't a one-off. Over the next two decades, hundreds of studies followed.

show.title: What the 2006 study showed
items: Testing beat rereading at one week
Students predicted that rereading would work better

segments.say: Skeptics asked a fair question. Perhaps testing helps with simple facts, but not with deeper understanding. In 2011, Jeffrey Karpicke and Janell Blunt set out to test that. They compared retrieval practice with a method that educators liked, called concept mapping, in which students draw diagrams of how ideas connect.

Eighty students read a science text, then either did retrieval practice, which meant writing down all they could remember, or drew concept maps while looking at the text. A week later, they took tests that asked for facts, and tests that asked for inferences. Retrieval practice won on both, including on the concept-mapping test itself.

show.what: Retrieval practice produces more learning than elaborative studying with concept mapping

segments.say: That result mattered. It suggested that retrieval practice doesn't only help with memorising facts. It also helps people to understand and apply what they've read. Recalling how ideas fit together seems to strengthen those connections, in a way that looking at a diagram doesn't.

Christopher Rowland combined results from many studies in a meta-analysis. He found a consistent benefit for testing over restudying, with a medium-sized effect, and that the benefit was larger when people got feedback on their answers. In other words, testing works, and it works better when you check what you got right and wrong.

show.what: The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: a meta-analytic review of the testing effect

segments.say: These are all versions of the same thing. Try to produce the answer before you look at it, then check. It doesn't need special equipment. A blank sheet, a set of flashcards or a friend with a list of questions is enough.

show.title: How to use retrieval practice
items: Close the book and write what you remember
Use flashcards, and say the answer before flipping

segments.say: Here's a finding that students tend to find reassuring. You don't even need to get the answer right for testing to help. In 2009, Nate Kornell, Matthew Hays and Robert Bjork asked people to study word pairs, and for some of them, to guess the answer before seeing it. Most of the guesses were wrong.

But the wrong guesses still helped. People who tried and failed to recall the answer, and then saw the right one, remembered it better later than people who simply studied the pair. The attempt seemed to prepare the mind to receive the answer. It's sometimes called pre-testing, and it suggests that a wrong guess isn't wasted.

show.where: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 2009
show.what: Unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance subsequent learning

segments.say: It turns the usual picture upside down. Many of us avoid questions that we can't answer, because failing feels bad. But trying and failing, followed by the correct answer, is an effective way to learn. It makes sense to try a problem before you've been taught the solution, and to guess a word before you look it up.

It also helps with something that everyone fears: being wrong. When errors are part of the method, they stop being embarrassing. They become information, and they point to exactly where more attention is needed.

show.title: Using the pretesting effect
items: Try a practice question before reading the chapter
Guess the meaning of a new word before checking
Predict the result before seeing an experiment
Note your errors and see what they teach you

segments.say: Testing works best when it's followed by feedback. If you practise an error without noticing, you may make it stronger. That's why checking your answers matters. In general, the research suggests that feedback soon after a test, and ideally with the correct answer shown, makes retrieval practice more effective.

There's a particularly interesting finding about errors that people make with high confidence. In 2012, Andrew Butler and Henry Roediger found that when students were confident but wrong, and then received feedback, they were more likely to correct the mistake than when they were unsure. A surprise seems to make the correction stick.

That fits with a general idea in psychology, that learning is driven by surprise. When the world doesn't match what you expected, the brain pays attention and updates. When it matches, there's little to learn. That's why a confident mistake, kindly corrected, can be one of the best learning moments there is.

show.where: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 2008
show.what: Correcting a metacognitive error: feedback increases retention of low-confidence correct responses

segments.say: It's worth saying that retrieval practice should be kind. It works best when the questions are challenging but achievable, and when you're gentle with yourself about the mistakes. A test that is far too hard just produces frustration. The sweet spot is a task where you get about two-thirds right, and learn from the rest.

Nothing complicated. A few minutes of recall after each session, a longer quiz at the end of the week and another a few weeks later. This is practice testing and spacing combined, and it's the closest the science of learning comes to a standard recipe.

show.title: A simple weekly routine
items: After each lesson, write down what you remember
At the end of the week, quiz yourself on it

segments.say: Flashcards are among the oldest tools in learning, and the research gives them a fresh seal of approval. Not because the cards are special, but because they make you recall. The card is a question, and the answer is yours to produce.

If you remember one thing from this chapter, remember that trying to recall is not a sign that you haven't learned. It's how you learn. The pause, the searching and the effort are the moments when memory is being built. Give them room.

So what did we learn? That retrieval practice beat rereading by about twenty points after a week. That it works for understanding as well as facts. That even failed attempts help, and that feedback makes it better. And that the feeling of difficulty is a good sign.
In our next chapter, we'll look at the second great method, and at a remarkable experiment in which a family of researchers tested their own memory for eight years.
